title: Democratizing Foundations of Problem-Solving with AI: A Breadth-First Search Curriculum for Middle School Students
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a curriculum that teaches Breadth-First Search (BFS) as a foundation for AI problem-solving can be successfully embedded into middle school science instruction and support both AI reasoning and related science learning. The authors are motivated by the broader problem that AI education is often delivered as stand-alone enrichment rather than integrated into subject-area coursework, limiting access and participation.

The intervention was a co-designed seven-day module implemented in a rural public middle school health science course. Students used i-SAIL, a Snap!-based interactive learning environment with custom AI blocks and visual simulations, alongside unplugged paper-based tracing tasks and hands-on science activities about virus transmission and contact tracing. The module linked BFS pathfinding to network-based science problems, including disease spread and hypothesizing about factors such as temperature and network density.

The study involved six classrooms across grades 6-8 in one U.S. middle school, with quantitative pre/post BFS assessments and worksheet artifacts from students, plus a post-implementation teacher interview. Results showed significant gains in BFS understanding from pre to post, many students could correctly trace BFS on a worksheet, and the teacher reported that the module fit well with the science unit and helped students understand both the science content and the AI ideas. The paper concludes that interactive, contextually grounded AI problem-solving can broaden access to AI learning in middle school science, though students still struggled with fully formal procedural tracing.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/classroom implementation study with pre/post analysis and no control group, so it provides useful but limited causal evidence. It is peer-reviewed style empirical work, but credibility is constrained by the small matched sample and lack of comparison condition.
impact_tier_rationale: The observed learning gain on BFS understanding was moderate (dz=0.453), which exceeds the threshold for modest-to-medium impact, but the evidence comes from a single small rural middle-school sample. The broader science achievement relevance is indirect because the measured outcomes are chiefly algorithmic/problem-solving understanding embedded in science instruction rather than a standardized science test.

interventions.use_case: middle school science-integrated instructional module using i-SAIL/Snap! with guided simulation-based BFS tracing, unplugged activities, and scaffolded practice for AI problem-solving

finding.finding_summary: Students showed improved understanding of BFS/problem-solving after the 4 core i-SAIL activities, with matched pre/post assessment scores increasing from M=0.683 to M=0.790 in the analyzed sample (n=41). The gain was statistically significant (paired t(40)=2.90, p=.006; Wilcoxon W=87, p=.008) with a moderate within-subject effect size of Cohen’s dz=0.453, on a 5-item BFS knowledge assessment targeting general search intuitions and BFS procedural understanding.
finding.measure: Matched pre/post BFS knowledge assessment (5 multiple-choice items on search intuition and BFS procedural understanding)

finding.finding_summary: On the paper-based BFS tracing worksheet, 64.5% of students accurately identified the shortest path to the goal state after instruction. However, many students omitted intermediate steps and exploration order details, indicating partial but emerging procedural competence rather than fully consistent scientific/inquiry-style reasoning about the algorithm.
finding.measure: Paper-based BFS tracing worksheet accuracy and completeness of step-by-step trace
